extracted.intended_audience: short-story writers, editors, anthology judges, and literary readers interested in how prize anthologies are chosen
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and personal selection criteria used by an anthology/judge when choosing short stories for a prize collection, including story-level qualities and how stories should work together in a collection. Emphasizes risks in language/structure, memorability, novelty, and invisible architecture of a collection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thrill or risk (language/structure/plot/enigma)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each story had to "show some sort of thrill or risk in terms of language or structure or plot or enigma; something in the story had to deliver a sharp blue jolt of electricity to my nervous system."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge privileges work that takes formal or linguistic risks rather than merely competent craft. Risk can be in language, structure, plot choices, or the presence of an enigma; the desired effect is a strong, immediate visceral reaction (a 'sharp blue jolt').

rubrics_metrics.name: Subversion of expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: "The second test was that each of the stories had to subvert my expectations..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories should surprise the reader and overturn predictable beats or familiar impulses of the form. Works that subvert the judge's own ingrained antipathies (e.g., disliked POVs or conventions) can still be accepted if they do something new or surprising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memorability over time
rubrics_metrics.description: "The final test for each story was that I had to remember it weeks and months after I first read it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A chosen story must linger in the reader's mind beyond initial reading. The judge used long-term recall as a filter, noting that some stories impress on first read but fail to remain memorable. Practical note: this criterion was used even through reading handicaps (e.g., COVID brain fog).

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty / doing something new
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories were selected when "the writer was doing something new," even when they used otherwise familiar modes (e.g., first person).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty and originality can override formal biases: a story in a commonly used POV or trope can be accepted if it reconfigures the form or presents fresh approaches. 'Doing something new' is a specific pathway for borderline or traditionally disliked choices to be included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point-of-view and voice daring (with exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge describes an aversion to overused POVs: "I asked Jenny to please stop sending me any more first-person stories..." and also notes second-person once 'smashed the aforementioned dislike to smithereens.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The judge is skeptical of repetitive POV choices (especially first person) because they can create solipsism, but is open to first- or second-person when the execution is inventive. POV is evaluated for whether it serves the story's risk/novelty and avoids numbing repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vitality and altering perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Selected stories often "throbbed with vitality, or made me see the familiar world as warped or strange."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories should feel alive and be capable of transforming how a reader perceives ordinary things. A strong, animating energy—voice, imagination, or moral/psychic intensity—is a key criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and emotional impact of the short form
rubrics_metrics.description: The short story form is "infinitely malleable, gorgeously economical, and endlessly surprising... long enough to lose oneself in, short enough to deliver a satisfying gut punch."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge values the formal economy unique to short fiction: compactness that nonetheless produces strong emotional or cognitive effects (a 'gut punch'). Efficiency of language and structural compression that still yields depth are positive attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invisible architecture and collection pacing
rubrics_metrics.description: The anthology should have an "invisible architecture... in which the first story asks a question or makes an argument, and this initial question or argument is then fractured and complicated by the next story, and so on, story by story, until the glorious grand finale."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assembling a collection, the judge considers order, thematic interplay, pacing, and how stories converse with each other. The editor builds the anthology slowly, balancing pieces against each other (like assembling a mixtape) to create emotional and intellectual progression toward a finale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Range of tonal/emotional aims and formal diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: The collection was assembled "to make you laugh, to bewilder and delight and scare you, to show... the extraordinary diversity of voice and journal and nationality and subject matter that the short story... encompasses."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An anthology should exhibit broad emotional registers and diverse formal/subject-matter representation: different voices, journals, nationalities, and tones enrich the collection and demonstrate the form's range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection process: iterative winnowing and balancing
rubrics_metrics.description: The judge describes building a 'maybe!' pile that grew, then a natural winnowing process and balancing pieces against one another to decide the final twenty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical editorial rubric: collect a large number of promising pieces, allow time and repeated comparison to test memorability and fit, and then thin the list by balancing strengths, tonal range, and how stories interact within the whole. Memorability and how a piece 'steps to its rhythms' were used during iterative selection.
